question.text: What are the steps for a right turn, and which lane do you turn from and into?

answer.text: Turn right from the lane furthest right: signal three or four seconds, one hundred feet, ahead, look left and right for pedestrians and traffic, brake before and during, stop fully at red lights and stop signs, and enter the lane closest to the curb unless markings lead otherwise.

teaching.text: Start in the lane furthest right, brake before and during the turn, and end in the curb lane. Remember: right from the right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn right from the lane furthest right: signal three or four seconds, one hundred feet, ahead, look left and right for pedestrians and traffic, brake before and during, stop fully at red lights and stop signs, and enter the lane closest to the curb unless markings lead otherwise.

question.text: What are the steps for a left turn, and which lane do you turn from and into?

answer.text: Turn left from the furthest left lane into the leftmost lane unless markings or multiple turn lanes direct otherwise: signal three or four seconds, one hundred feet, ahead, look all ways including opposite traffic, hold wheels straight until committed, and yield to opposite vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians.

teaching.text: Start in the furthest left lane, keep the wheels straight until committed, and end in the leftmost lane. Remember: left from the left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn left from the furthest left lane into the leftmost lane unless markings or multiple turn lanes direct otherwise: signal three or four seconds, one hundred feet, ahead, look all ways including opposite traffic, hold wheels straight until committed, and yield to opposite vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians.

question.text: How do the starting and ending lanes differ for right and left turns?

answer.text: Right turns start furthest right and end curb-side, while left turns start furthest left and end leftmost.

teaching.text: Right starts right and ends at the curb; left starts left and ends leftmost. Remember: right curbside, left leftmost.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Right turns start furthest right and end curb-side, while left turns start furthest left and end leftmost.

question.text: How do two opposing vehicles that are both turning left pass each other?

answer.text: Two opposing vehicles signaling left turns pass in front of each other with their passenger sides beside each other.

teaching.text: Opposing left-turners pass in front of each other, passenger side to passenger side. Remember: passenger sides side by side.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Two opposing vehicles signaling left turns pass in front of each other with their passenger sides beside each other.

question.text: What should you check before a U-turn, and where are U-turns allowed?

answer.text: Before any U-turn, check for No U-Turn or No Left Turn signs; in business districts, cities, and towns U-turns are allowed only at intersections, and never on a highway.

teaching.text: Check the signs, use an intersection in town, and never U-turn on a highway. Remember: signs, intersections, never highway.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before any U-turn, check for No U-Turn or No Left Turn signs; in business districts, cities, and towns U-turns are allowed only at intersections, and never on a highway.

question.text: Which conditions can each ban a U-turn on their own?

answer.text: U-turns need clear signs, town intersections, and no highway; each condition bans them alone.

teaching.text: Any one missing condition bans the U-turn: signs, a town intersection, or a road that is not a highway. Remember: any one bans it.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: U-turns need clear signs, town intersections, and no highway; each condition bans them alone.

question.text: What are the steps for making a U-turn?

answer.text: To U-turn, signal left, stop, yield to approaching traffic, and when clear enter the outside or right-hand lane of the opposite direction.

teaching.text: A U-turn adds a stop and a yield, and it ends in the right-hand lane of the opposite direction. Remember: signal, stop, yield, right lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To U-turn, signal left, stop, yield to approaching traffic, and when clear enter the outside or right-hand lane of the opposite direction.

question.text: How does a U-turn differ from a left turn in stopping and yielding?

answer.text: U-turns add a full stop and yield before entering the far lane, while left turns yield without stopping.

teaching.text: The U-turn adds a full stop that a left turn does not. Remember: U-turn adds a stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: U-turns add a full stop and yield before entering the far lane, while left turns yield without stopping.

question.text: When does the law require turn signals, and must you signal with no traffic around?

answer.text: Turn signals are required by law for lane changes, turns, and highway entries and exits; use them or hand signals even with no traffic around, and cancel the signal after finishing.

teaching.text: Signals are required even on an empty road, and you cancel them when the move is done. Remember: always signal, then cancel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn signals are required by law for lane changes, turns, and highway entries and exits; use them or hand signals even with no traffic around, and cancel the signal after finishing.

question.text: How far ahead of a turn should you signal?

answer.text: Signal three or four seconds, one hundred feet, before your turn, and stay alert for drivers who may pull out misjudging where you will turn.

teaching.text: Signal three or four seconds ahead, and watch for drivers who misjudge where you will turn. Remember: three or four seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal three or four seconds, one hundred feet, before your turn, and stay alert for drivers who may pull out misjudging where you will turn.

question.text: When do signals start, and what must you do after the move?

answer.text: Signals open three to four seconds ahead of the move and must be canceled after it.

teaching.text: Open the signal early and close it after the move. Remember: signal early, then cancel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signals open three to four seconds ahead of the move and must be canceled after it.

question.text: What are the three hand signals?

answer.text: Hand signals use the left arm: straight out for a left turn, pointing up for a right turn, and pointing down for slowing or stopping.

teaching.text: All three hand signals use the left arm: straight for left, up for right, down for slowing or stopping. Remember: straight, up, down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand signals use the left arm: straight out for a left turn, pointing up for a right turn, and pointing down for slowing or stopping.

question.text: What does each left-arm position mean?

answer.text: Left arm straight means left, left arm up means right, and left arm down means slow or stop.

teaching.text: Straight is left, up is a right turn, down is slow or stop. Remember: straight left, up right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Left arm straight means left, left arm up means right, and left arm down means slow or stop.

question.text: What is over-correcting, and how do you recover if you veer off the road?

answer.text: Over-correcting steers more sharply than expected and slides the rear wheels outward, risking control loss; slow down on curves, and if you veer off, ease off speed without panic, look where you want to go, and steer back slowly.

teaching.text: Sharp steering slides the rear wheels; ease off, look where you want to go and steer back slowly. Remember: ease off, look, steer back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Over-correcting steers more sharply than expected and slides the rear wheels outward, risking control loss; slow down on curves, and if you veer off, ease off speed without panic, look where you want to go, and steer back slowly.

question.text: What causes over-correction, and what does recovery involve?

answer.text: Over-correction slides the rear out from sharp steering, and recovery means easing speed, aiming eyes, and steering back slowly.

teaching.text: Sharp steering causes the slide; slow, calm steering is the recovery. Remember: sharp steer slides rear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Over-correction slides the rear out from sharp steering, and recovery means easing speed, aiming eyes, and steering back slowly.

question.text: How do you build a space cushion?

answer.text: Build a space cushion by centering your lane and keeping room ahead and behind so vehicles can pass or stop safely.

teaching.text: Centering your lane with room ahead and behind lets other vehicles pass or stop safely. Remember: center lane, room around.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Build a space cushion by centering your lane and keeping room ahead and behind so vehicles can pass or stop safely.

question.text: On dry roads, how many seconds should you follow at different speeds?

answer.text: On dry roads follow at two seconds under thirty-five miles per hour, three seconds from thirty-five to forty-five, and four seconds from forty-six to seventy; the rule fails above seventy.

teaching.text: Two seconds under thirty-five, three up to forty-five, four up to seventy, and the rule fails above seventy. Remember: two, three, four seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On dry roads follow at two seconds under thirty-five miles per hour, three seconds from thirty-five to forty-five, and four seconds from forty-six to seventy; the rule fails above seventy.

question.text: Which following gap serves each speed band?

answer.text: Two seconds serve under thirty-five, three serve thirty-five to forty-five, four serve forty-six to seventy, and none serve above seventy.

teaching.text: Each speed band adds a second, from two up to four, with no rule above seventy. Remember: bands of two to four.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Two seconds serve under thirty-five, three serve thirty-five to forty-five, four serve forty-six to seventy, and none serve above seventy.

question.text: How do you time your following gap, and when should you add seconds?

answer.text: Time your gap from a fixed object the car ahead passes: arriving early means too close, so slow and widen; add seconds for bad weather, heavy traffic, poor pavement, or a poor vehicle.

teaching.text: Arriving at the fixed object before your count ends means you are too close. Remember: count from a fixed object.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Time your gap from a fixed object the car ahead passes: arriving early means too close, so slow and widen; add seconds for bad weather, heavy traffic, poor pavement, or a poor vehicle.

question.text: How long do hand and foot responses take, and what changes stopping?

answer.text: Hand response runs near a half second and foot response near three-quarters, before perception delays from tiredness, medication, or distraction; conditions, speed, alertness, and vehicle weight all change stopping.

teaching.text: Feet respond more slowly than hands, and tiredness, medication or distraction add more delay. Remember: half second, three-quarters.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand response runs near a half second and foot response near three-quarters, before perception delays from tiredness, medication, or distraction; conditions, speed, alertness, and vehicle weight all change stopping.

question.text: How do hand and foot response times compare?

answer.text: Hands answer in about a half second and feet in about three-quarters, before tiredness, medication, or distraction add more.

teaching.text: About a half second for hands and three-quarters for feet, before other delays. Remember: hands faster than feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hands answer in about a half second and feet in about three-quarters, before tiredness, medication, or distraction add more.

question.text: When should you widen your following distance?

answer.text: Widen following distance behind vision-blocking large vehicles, in bad weather or heavy traffic, when exiting expressways, behind motorcycles or bicycles, and when being tailgated.

teaching.text: Large vehicles, bad weather, heavy traffic, expressway exits, bikes and tailgaters all call for more room. Remember: more room behind trucks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Widen following distance behind vision-blocking large vehicles, in bad weather or heavy traffic, when exiting expressways, behind motorcycles or bicycles, and when being tailgated.

question.text: How does timing the gap differ from widening it?

answer.text: Fixed-object timing detects a short gap, while large vehicles, weather, exits, small bikes, and tailgaters demand a longer one.

teaching.text: Timing tells you the gap is too short; the list tells you when to add more. Remember: time it, then widen.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Fixed-object timing detects a short gap, while large vehicles, weather, exits, small bikes, and tailgaters demand a longer one.

question.text: What should you do when you are being tailgated?

answer.text: When tailgated, never brake suddenly: move over or tap the brakes to flash and slow; help followers with a steady speed and brake taps before slowing or stopping.

teaching.text: Never brake suddenly when tailgated; move over or tap the brakes to flash and slow. Remember: never brake suddenly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When tailgated, never brake suddenly: move over or tap the brakes to flash and slow; help followers with a steady speed and brake taps before slowing or stopping.

question.text: How does a tailgated driver's response differ from a considerate driver's habit?

answer.text: The tailgated driver moves over or flashes brakes to slow, while the considerate driver holds steady speed with early brake taps.

teaching.text: Tailgated drivers move over or flash and slow; considerate drivers hold a steady speed and tap early. Remember: move over or tap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The tailgated driver moves over or flashes brakes to slow, while the considerate driver holds steady speed with early brake taps.

question.text: How far ahead should you focus, and how should you search the scene?

answer.text: Search the whole scene with moving eyes, focus twenty to thirty seconds ahead or about one city block, and scan side to side for signs, signals, cars, and people.

teaching.text: Focus about one city block ahead and keep your eyes moving side to side. Remember: one block ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Search the whole scene with moving eyes, focus twenty to thirty seconds ahead or about one city block, and scan side to side for signs, signals, cars, and people.

question.text: What road clues should you watch for, in town and in rural areas?

answer.text: Read road clues like exhaust smoke, brake or backup lights, and turned wheels; watch for pedestrians, bicyclists, and slow vehicles, and in rural areas for hidden junctions, curves, hills, trucks, and farm equipment.

teaching.text: Smoke, brake or backup lights and turned wheels are clues to read, along with people, bikes and slow vehicles. Remember: smoke, lights, wheels.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Read road clues like exhaust smoke, brake or backup lights, and turned wheels; watch for pedestrians, bicyclists, and slow vehicles, and in rural areas for hidden junctions, curves, hills, trucks, and farm equipment.

question.text: How should you look when entering an intersection, and how often should you check the rearview mirror?

answer.text: Enter intersections with a left-right-left look, left first as the nearer threat; check the rearview about every ten seconds and before lane changes, backing, quick slows, and long descents.

teaching.text: Left first at intersections, then right, then left again; check the mirror about every ten seconds. Remember: left, right, left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Enter intersections with a left-right-left look, left first as the nearer threat; check the rearview about every ten seconds and before lane changes, backing, quick slows, and long descents.

question.text: How far ahead do your eyes go, how often do you check mirrors, and how do you enter intersections?

answer.text: Eyes run twenty to thirty seconds ahead, mirrors check about every ten seconds, and intersections get left-right-left.

teaching.text: Eyes far ahead, mirror about every ten seconds, left first at intersections. Remember: ahead, mirror, left first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Eyes run twenty to thirty seconds ahead, mirrors check about every ten seconds, and intersections get left-right-left.
